questions.prompt: A loop gain with a single pole in the open left half-plane cannot oscillate under negative feedback because
options: its phase reaches \(-180^\circ\) at a finite frequency
its magnitude is constant
a single pole never contributes \(180^\circ\) of lag
negative feedback removes every pole
questions.explanation: One real pole contributes a phase between \(0^\circ\) and \(-90^\circ\). Oscillation needs the phase at \(-180^\circ\) while the magnitude is at least \(1\). The pole does not hold the magnitude constant, and feedback does not delete it.

questions.prompt: At the frequency where \(|L| = 1\), the phase of \(L\) is \(-140^\circ\). What is the phase margin, in degrees?
questions.explanation: Phase margin is \(180^\circ\) plus the phase at gain crossover: \(180-140 = 40\). The phase \(-140^\circ\) is not the margin. Subtracting the phase from \(90^\circ\) gives \(50\), which drops half of the \(180^\circ\).

questions.prompt: A negative-feedback loop oscillates at a frequency where
options: \(|L| = 1\) and the phase is \(0^\circ\)
\(|L| = 1\) and the phase is \(-180^\circ\)
the phase is \(-180^\circ\) and \(|L|\) is below \(1\)
\(|L|\) is large and the phase is \(-90^\circ\)
questions.explanation: Oscillation needs the return to add, which is phase \(-180^\circ\), and to have magnitude \(1\), so the signal sustains itself. Phase \(0^\circ\) is still subtracting. Magnitude below \(1\) at \(-180^\circ\) dies out. Phase \(-90^\circ\) is the lag of one pole, not the oscillation condition.

questions.prompt: The phase of \(L\) reaches \(-180^\circ\) at a frequency where \(|L| = 0.25\). What is the gain margin, as a factor?
questions.explanation: The gain margin is \(1/|L|\) at the phase crossover: \(1/0.25 = 4\). The loop could be multiplied by \(4\) before \(|L|\) hits \(1\) at \(-180^\circ\). The value \(0.25\) is the present magnitude, not the margin.

questions.prompt: At gain crossover the phase of the loop gain is phi degrees, and phi is negative. Write the phase margin in degrees, using the name phi.
questions.explanation: Phase margin is \(180+\phi\) when \(\phi\) is the phase in degrees at \(|L|=1\). Using \(-\phi\) reports the lag, not the distance to \(-180^\circ\). Using \(90+\phi\) drops half of the full inversion.

options: how much phase remains at the frequency where \(|L|=1\)
the frequency where the phase is \(-180^\circ\)
how much the loop gain can rise before \(|L|=1\) at phase \(-180^\circ\)
the closed-loop gain at DC
questions.explanation: Gain margin is read at the phase crossover, and it is the factor \(1/|L|\) there. The spare phase at magnitude \(1\) is the phase margin. The crossover frequency is not a margin, and the DC closed-loop gain is a different number.

questions.prompt: Order the reading of the two margins from a loop gain.
questions.explanation: Phase margin is tied to the magnitude crossing, and gain margin is tied to the phase crossing. Swapping those two frequencies swaps the margins. The reciprocal of the phase is not a gain.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 186" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>loop gain falling as frequency rises</title><line x1="50" y1="156" x2="300" y2="156"/><polygon points="300,156 293.6,158.7 293.6,153.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="50" y1="156" x2="50" y2="30"/><polygon points="50,30 52.7,36.4 47.3,36.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="300" y="172" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">log ω</text><text x="54" y="26" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">|H| dB</text><polyline points="58,42 150,86 268,142" stroke-width="2.2"/><text x="96" y="52" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−20</text><text x="188" y="96" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">−40</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A magnitude sketch that falls, then falls more steeply.
steps: Read the phase there and add it to \(180^\circ\) to get the phase margin.
Find the frequency where the phase is \(-180^\circ\).
Take the reciprocal of \(|L|\) there to get the gain margin.

questions.prompt: At the frequency where the phase is \(-180^\circ\), \(|L| = 0.5\). What is the gain margin in dB?
questions.explanation: The factor is \(1/0.5 = 2\), and \(20\log_{10}(2)\) is about \(6.02\) dB. Reporting \(0.5\) dB uses the magnitude as if it were already in decibels. A factor of \(0.5\) would be a loss, not the room the gain still has.

questions.prompt: A note reads margins. The phase at \(|L|=1\) is \(-140^\circ\), and \(|L|=0.5\) where the phase is \(-180^\circ\). Exactly one step is wrong.
questions.explanation: The gain margin is \(1/|L|\), not \(|L|\). Here that factor is \(2\). The phase margin really is \(40^\circ\), and the two crossover definitions in the other steps are right.

steps: Gain crossover is the frequency where \(|L|=1\).
Phase crossover is the frequency where the phase is \(-180^\circ\).
The gain margin is \(0.5\), the value of \(|L|\) at that frequency.

questions.prompt: Preview of choosing a margin. At gain crossover the phase is \(-125^\circ\). What is the phase margin, in degrees?
questions.explanation: The phase margin is \(180-125 = 55\). A later skill decides whether a margin of that size is enough, and how much delay it can buy. The phase \(-125^\circ\) is the reading, not the margin.

questions.prompt: Preview of robust stability. At the frequency where the phase is \(-180^\circ\), \(|L| = 0.2\). The loop is
options: unstable, because the phase reached \(-180^\circ\)
stable, with a gain margin of \(5\)
stable only if the phase margin is zero
oscillating at that frequency
questions.explanation: Magnitude \(0.2\) at \(-180^\circ\) means the gain would have to rise by a factor \(5\) before the oscillation condition is met. Reaching \(-180^\circ\) is not by itself instability. A later skill measures the distance of the frequency-response curve from \(-1\), which this margin is a slice of.

questions.prompt: Preview of a second pole. Which statements are true of a loop whose \(L(s)\) has only one pole, in the open left half-plane?
options: The phase stays above \(-180^\circ\).
The gain margin is infinite, because the phase never reaches \(-180^\circ\).
The phase reaches \(-180^\circ\) at a high enough frequency.
Phase margin is read at the frequency where the phase is \(-180^\circ\).
questions.explanation: One pole contributes less than \(180^\circ\) of lag, so there is no phase crossover and the gain margin is infinite. A second pole is what lets an amplifier loop reach \(-180^\circ\), and placing that pole is a later skill. Phase margin is read where \(|L|=1\), not where the phase is \(-180^\circ\).
